u10-l01.title: The king that has not castled
u10-l01.summary: A king in the center is a target

u10-l01-s01.text: The white king is still on f1 without having castled, and its pieces don't protect it well. With Qh1+ Black forces the queen trade, the rook recaptures on h1 with check, the king has to go to f2 and the rook captures on d1. A king that has not castled gives checks the time they need.

u10-l01-s02.text: The black king is on d8 without having castled. With Qh8+ White forces the bishop to interpose, with Rd1+ sends the king to c8 and the queen captures the bishop on e8 with check. Each check takes a square away from the king.

u10-l01-s03.prompt: Which of these two kings has not castled?
u10-l01-s03.explanation: The black king is still on d8, in the center, and White has already put theirs safe on c1.
feedback: The white king has already castled long: it is on c1, behind its pawns.
One of the two is still in the center.

u10-l02-s01.text: With both kings castled kingside, the attack usually goes against the h pawn (h7 or h2). Here Bxh7+ gives check and, as the bishop leaves d3, the white queen on d1 sees the black queen on d6: the king captures the bishop and Qxd6 wins the queen.

u10-l02-s02.text: The f7, g7 and h7 pawns are the black king's shield, and the queen together with the bishop on c2 aim at h7. Qxh7+ forces the king to f8 and Qh8 is mate.

u10-l02-s03.prompt: How many black pieces defend the h7 pawn?
u10-l02-s03.explanation: The king on g8 and the knight on f6 defend it: two defenders. Before attacking, count attackers and defenders.
feedback: Count again: besides the king, look at which other black piece reaches h7.
Count again: it is fewer than three.

u10-l03.title: Opposite-side castling
u10-l03.summary: Each side attacks the other's king

u10-l03-s01.text: The kings are on opposite wings: White's on b1 and Black's on g8. Black attacks on the queenside: Qxa2+ gives check, the king goes to c1 and Qa1 is mate. With opposite-side castling each side attacks the other's king and whoever arrives first wins.

u10-l03-s02.text: Here the black king is on c8 and the white king on g1. White attacks on the queenside: Qxb7# is mate because the rook on b1 protects the queen and the king cannot capture it.

u10-l03-s03.prompt: With opposite-side castling, what is usually best?
options: Moving the pawns that protect your own king
Trading all the pieces as soon as possible
Throwing pawns and pieces at the enemy king
u10-l03-s03.explanation: Each side attacks the other's king: whoever arrives first wins. Pawns are thrown toward the enemy king, not toward your own.
feedback: Moving the pawns of your castled position weakens your own king just when the opponent attacks.
Trading pieces puts out the attack and leaves both sides without play against the king.

u10-l03-s04.hint: One is on the queenside and the other on the kingside.

u10-l03-s05.hint: Look for the capture that leaves the king without its protection.
u10-l03-s05.success: Correct. Rxc7# attacks the queenside king.

u10-l03-s06.success: Correct. Nxd6+ attacks the queenside king.

u10-l04-s01.text: White gives check with Qd7+. Black doesn't run with the king: they interpose the rook on c7, protected by the king. If the queen captures, the king recaptures and the attacking piece disappears.

u10-l04-s02.text: Black gives check with the queen on a2. White interposes the rook on c2, protected by the king: the queen has to capture it and the king recaptures.

u10-l04-s03.prompt: Which piece protects the rook that interposes on c7?

u10-l05-s01.text: When you have less material, you don't need to win: you need a draw. The black king on a8 has no squares and is not in check. It is stalemated, and the game ends in a draw.

u10-l05-s02.text: Perpetual check is another lifeline: if your queen can check again and again, the opponent has no time to progress. Sometimes the position repeats and the game is a draw.

u10-l05-s03.prompt: What are you looking for when you have less material?
u10-l05-s03.explanation: With less material, the goal is not to lose. Perpetual check, stalemate, and fortress are resources to save a half point.
options: Draw: perpetual check, stalemate, or fortress
feedback: Changing pieces doesn't always help if you are still down in material.
Attacking usually loses: the rival has more strength.

u10-l05-s04.prompt: Tap the three squares that control the black king.
u10-l05-s04.hint: The queen and the white king cover the three escape squares.

u10-l05-s05.explanation: In a fortress, the extra material is useless because the rival cannot enter. It is another way to draw.
options: A position the rival cannot break even with more material
feedback: A fortress is defensive, not an attack.
Changing pieces does not define a fortress.

u10-l05-s06.text: Summary: with less material, look for a draw. Stalemate, perpetual check, and fortress are your three resources. You don't need to win; you need not to lose.

u10-l06.title: Converting an Advantage
u10-l06.summary: Simplify without giving away the win

u10-l06-s01.text: White has an extra bishop. The plan is simple: exchange pieces, not pawns, bring the king to the center in the endgame, and prevent the opponent from getting counterplay.

u10-l06-s02.text: Exchanging queens reduces the opponent's chances. After an exchange, your material advantage is more noticeable and the endgame is easier to play.

u10-l06-s03.prompt: When you are winning, what do you exchange?
u10-l06-s03.explanation: Exchanging pieces reduces counterplay. Exchanging pawns can leave the opponent with a passed pawn or an easier defense.
feedback: Exchanging pawns can lead to a draw for the opponent.
It's not advisable to exchange everything: aim to simplify, not give away the advantage.

u10-l06-s04.prompt: What do you avoid when you have an advantage?
u10-l06-s04.explanation: With an advantage, the opponent needs complications. You seek the opposite: fewer pieces and a clear endgame.
feedback: Simplifying is exactly what you want.
Activating the king is good in the endgame.

u10-l06-s05.hint: Your queen and the opponent's queen are on the d-file. Capture theirs.
u10-l06-s05.success: Correct. After Rxd8, you are left with rook and bishop against rook: a winning endgame.

u10-l06-s06.text: Summary: with an advantage, simplify. Exchange pieces, not pawns; activate the king and avoid opening the game unnecessarily. Victory is built with patience.

u10-l07.title: Making a plan
u10-l07.summary: Choosing the idea before the move

u10-l07-s01.text: Before moving, choose a plan. Ask yourself what your worst piece is, where you have more space, and what weakness you can attack. The move comes after the idea.

u10-l07-s02.text: Here White has more space in the center. A typical plan is to improve the bishop on c1, which is behind its pawns, and then attack the kingside. Pieces first, pawns later.

u10-l07-s03.prompt: What plan makes the most sense here?
u10-l07-s03.explanation: With more space, the plan is to develop the worst piece and attack where you have an advantage. The bishop on c1 is the piece to improve.
options: Improve the bishop on c1 and attack the kingside
feedback: Changing everything doesn't utilize your space.
Moving the castling pawns weakens your own king.

u10-l07-s04.prompt: Tap the square of the white piece that needs improvement.
u10-l07-s04.hint: It is the bishop behind its own pawns.

u10-l07-s05.prompt: What question do you ask yourself before moving?
u10-l07-s05.explanation: A plan starts with the position: the worst piece, the space, and the opponent's weaknesses.
options: What is my worst piece and where do I have an advantage?
How do I change all the pieces?
feedback: Looking for sacrifices without a plan is starting from the end.
Changing everything is not a plan in itself.

u10-l07-s06.text: Summary: first the plan, then the move. Improve your worst piece, attack where you have space, and create a weakness in the opponent's field. A plan lasts several moves.
